🌍 Europe Regional Context (applies across all European destinations)

🧭 General Trip Structure

  • Multi-country itineraries are common in Europe → may require multiple DMCs on one trip
  • Higher degree of customization is typical
  • ⚠️ Don't over-rely on DMCs during the quoting process
  • North American clients typically arrive in the morning — check if they want an extra hotel night for early check-in
  • Departures vary — always confirm where the client's trip actually ends

🚐 Driver/Guide Combinations (exam-likely — know these distinctions)

Term What's Included
Vehicle/Driver/Guide Separate driver AND guide
Vehicle/Driver-Guide (Vehicle/Tourism Driver) ONE person does both roles
Guide/Taxi Local guide + taxis/public transit for transport
Driver/Vehicle Driver only, NO guide — may not speak English in some destinations
  • Circuit touring exists in some regions

🔄 Transfers

  • Often via public transit (trains, ferries, etc.)
  • Use reputable trains specific to the country — e.g., no local trains in Germany/Italy, though local trains may be fine in Norway
  • Be aware of public transit strikes — know how to communicate to clients and pivot
  • Porterage is not always available
  • Drivers often have limits on how far they can accompany clients on public transit
  • Private transfers are often routed through an interesting stop/site to break up the drive

🏨 Hotels

  • ⚠️ Do NOT book "lead-in"/standard rooms — these are much smaller than North American standard rooms
  • Room sizes and "star levels" differ from North America
  • Air conditioning is not always offered
  • Elevators may not be available in historical buildings
  • City tax is sometimes due at check-out

🚶 Touring

  • Can be history-heavy — balance full-day, half-day, hands-on experiences, and downtime based on client interests

✏️ Customizing

  • Account for where the guide/driver starts and ends when estimating pricing
  • Check country-specific driver rules: work hours, required breaks, overnight supplements
  • Google Maps drive times are estimates only — not exact

🛂 Visa/Entry Requirements (exam-likely — specific numbers)

Last verified: August 26, 2026 — entry-requirement timelines have shifted repeatedly; re-check the official sites below before relying on any date here for a live client conversation.

ETIAS (Europe):

  • ⚠️ Not yet in effect, and no confirmed launch date. ETIAS was expected in Q4 2026, but that target was quietly removed from the official EU site in mid-2026 after the agency building it (eu-LISA) concluded a 2026 launch wasn't feasible — a 2027 launch is now considered the likely outcome. Don't quote clients a specific ETIAS date; direct them to check travel-europe.europa.eu/etias closer to travel
  • Once live, it will require pre-travel authorization for ~1.4 billion travelers from 60+ visa-exempt countries, for short stays in 30 European countries
  • EES (Entry/Exit System) — the separate biometric border system ETIAS was waiting on — is fully operational as of April 10, 2026. Clients should expect fingerprint + facial scan at Schengen borders now (replacing the passport stamp), which can add time at busy airports — mention this regardless of ETIAS's status

UK ETA (affects US & Canadian clients):

  • Rolled out in phases from late 2023; hard, mandatory enforcement began February 25, 2026 — airlines, ferries, and Eurostar are now required to verify ETA status before boarding, with no exceptions
  • Applies to ALL travelers, including children/infants, and those transiting without going through border control — every traveler needs their own individual ETA (no family/group applications)
  • Processing time: typically minutes to ~3 days (recommend applying 2+ weeks ahead regardless)
  • Valid for 2 years, multiple entries, covering unlimited visits of up to 6 months each
  • Requirements: passport being traveled with, email, credit card, uploaded passport copy + photo
  • Cost: £16 (rose from the original £10 in April 2025; a further increase to £20 has been proposed by the Home Office but a confirmed effective date isn't verified as of this writing — double-check current pricing before quoting a client)
  • Official site: gov.uk/guidance/apply-for-an-electronic-travel-authorisation-eta

SPAIN — PASSPORT & VISA INFORMATION

(Spain-specific — separate from the general Europe/ETIAS/UK ETA notes in Section 0)

Passport Validity

  • Non-Schengen international travelers: passport must be valid for at least 3 months after the end of the trip to enter the Schengen zone
  • Schengen citizens: no passport required, but must carry valid ID

Visa-Free Entry to Spain (90 days)

  • Citizens of: Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Malaysia, Israel, UAE, and most of North America can visit visa-free for up to 90 days
  • If unsure → recommend client contact their embassy/consulate

ETIAS (status as of August 2026 — not yet in effect)

  • 60+ visa-exempt countries' citizens will require an ETA (ETIAS) to enter 30 specific European countries (including Spain) for short stays up to 90 days — once it launches
  • ⚠️ Not live yet, and no confirmed date — the previously-targeted Q4 2026 launch was quietly dropped by the EU in mid-2026; a 2027 launch is now considered more likely. See Section 0 for the fuller status
  • ETIAS is NOT a visa, NOT a passport, and will NOT guarantee entry — it's only pre-authorization
  • Direct clients to travel-europe.europa.eu/etias to confirm current requirements before departure — don't rely on a memorized date

Canada-Specific Note

  • Canadian passport holders do not need a Schengen visa for tourism/business/study in Spain if stay is under 90 days within any 180-day period (includes time in other Schengen countries) — this is a stable Schengen-wide rule, unaffected by ETIAS's delayed timeline
  • Customs may ask for proof of sufficient funds — cash, certified cheques, or credit card + current statement

⚠️ Important Reminder

  • Entry/exit requirements are constantly evolving — always verify current rules rather than relying on memorized info
  • Sherpa (partner tool) can be used to determine visa/entry requirements per destination and to apply for visas

🔑 SPAIN — KEY LOCALES OVERVIEW

Regional Structure (exam-likely — number of communities) - Spain is divided into 17 autonomous communities - Kensington's top locales fall within three of these: Madrid (the community), Catalonia (Cataluña/Catalunya), and Andalusia (Andalucía)

Madrid & Catalonia

  • Covered in depth in Sections 1.2 (Madrid) and 1.4 (Barcelona) above

Andalusia (Andalucía)

  • The region most associated with classic Spanish imagery: bullfighting, flamenco dancing, guitar playing — the "quintessential culture of Spain"
  • Contains Seville, Córdoba, Granada, Marbella (all covered via the Job Aid sections 1.6–1.10 above)

Locale ↔ Site Matching Reference (exam-likely — this exact pairing exercise appeared in the course) | Site | Locale | |---|---| | Prado Museum | Madrid | | Picasso Museum | Barcelona | | Royal Alcázar | Seville | | Mezquita-Cathedral | Córdoba | | Alhambra Palace | Granada | | La Concha (mountain) | Marbella — the distinctive shell-shaped mountain (part of the Sierra Blanca) that backdrops Marbella |

🏨 SPAIN — HOTEL BOOKING RULES (Job Aid)

General selection rules, Parador requests, Discovery/Premier sequencing and Andalusia room configuration. Hotel-by-hotel picks now live inside each city section.

  • Location: Spanish city centers are great for exploring on foot during leisure time; most preferred hotels are conveniently close to attractions, shopping, dining
  • Historic vs. Modern: many properties are renovated historic buildings — set client expectations that these often have smaller rooms; check if the client has a preference for a modern hotel instead

Paradors — client requests (exam-likely — what to offer instead) - Paradors = government-owned historic properties (castles, palaces, historic monuments), often in remote locations, offering an authentic cultural experience - Only a few Paradors are built into TMT — they generally lack the modern amenities/convenient locations of KT's preferred hotels - If a client requests a Parador, two options: 1. Offer a Hospes hotel instead — also unique historic properties, but more centrally located, with modern amenities, part of Design Hotels by Marriott Bonvoy (ties to multiple Hospes properties already noted in the hotel tables below) 2. If they still want the Parador specifically: set clear expectations about the services/amenities trade-off

Discovery-Level Properties (exam-likely — sequencing logic for mixed-level itineraries) - Not every locale has a Discovery-level property available - For price-conscious clients mixing levels: ⚠️ start the itinerary with Discovery, end with Premier — never the reverse (starting Premier then downgrading to Discovery risks disappointing the client) - Example: NH Collection Madrid Gran Vía (Discovery, Madrid) as the first hotel → NH Sevilla Plaza de Armas (Premier, Seville) later in the trip — same hotel brand/style maintained, but service level elevates as the trip progresses

Andalusia — Room Configuration Considerations (applies to Seville, Granada, Córdoba)

  • Many preferred Andalusia hotels are historic and lack quad or connecting room options — challenging for family bookings
  • 💡 Group of 4+: look for adjoining rooms (not the same as connecting)
  • 💡 Family with young children: check the hotel's definition of "adult" (typically ~12+) — e.g., 2 adults + an 11-year-old can often fit in one room

🏛️ MADRID

Tap to flip
mah-DRID

Orientation

  • Central Madrid is smaller/more walkable than it appears
  • Puerta del Sol — the city's bustling central intersection; all distances in Spain are measured from here (exam-likely fact)

Key Neighborhoods

Neighborhood Location Character
Sol Heart of Madrid One of the busiest/most iconic areas; home to Puerta del Sol square (central meeting point) and Plaza Mayor; shopping, dining, entertainment, narrow streets of shops/cafés
Los Austrias South of Calle Mayor Oldest area of Madrid; home to Palacio Real (Royal Palace) and Plaza Mayor
(Unnamed triangle: Cibeles/Atocha/Sol) East/south of Sol Restaurants & bars; home to Madrid's three renowned museums and Parque del Buen Retiro
Lavapiés Just south of Sol Formerly working-class; now ethnically diverse (African & Asian immigrant influx)
Malasaña North of Sol, across Gran Vía Alternative/bohemian vibe; popular with artists, musicians, young people; colorful street art, vintage/eclectic boutiques, lively nightlife; Calle Fuencarral — must-visit for fashion
Chueca North of Sol, across Gran Vía Madrid's LGBTQ+ district; open-minded atmosphere, vibrant nightlife, trendy bars/clubs; fashionable boutiques & cultural venues by day; hosts annual Pride celebrations
La Latina — Historic; traditional Spanish taverns & tapas bars; home to El Rastro flea market (Sundays); San Francisco el Grande Basilica; narrow streets
Barrio de las Letras (Literary Quarter) — Once home to writers Cervantes and Lope de Vega; cobblestone streets, literary landmarks, art galleries, cozy cafés; Huertas street — known for nightlife/cultural events
Retiro Adjacent to El Retiro Park Peaceful retreat from city center; park gardens, boating lake, Crystal Palace; near Prado Museum & other cultural sites

Note: "the three renowned museums" — see confirmation/detail under Key Attractions → Paseo del Arte below. Note: El Rastro flea market (see Shopping section) is confirmed to run on Sundays.

Airport (exam-likely — official name & key facts)

  • Official name: Adolfo Suárez Madrid–Barajas Airport
  • Spain's busiest and largest airport; major gateway to the Iberian Peninsula
  • Location: ~10 km northeast of city center
  • Named after former Spanish PM Adolfo Suárez
  • Website: aena.es/en/adolfo-suarez-madrid-barajas.html
  • Facilities: international/domestic terminals, duty-free shopping, dining, VIP lounges, taxis/bus/metro connections, currency exchange, ATMs, baggage services, car rental
  • Fun fact: one of the largest airport art collections in the world — 1,000+ pieces (sculptures, paintings, installations)

Airport → City Center Options

Option Details
Airport Express Bus (Line 203) Connects airport to Atocha Railway Station & Plaza de Cibeles; ~30–40 min; fare ~€5; buy from driver or vending machine
Metro Available — see city metro details below
Taxi Metered, regulated fares
Private Transfer/Shuttle Door-to-door option

Getting Around Madrid

Mode Key Facts
Metro One of the most extensive/efficient systems in the world — 12 lines, 300+ stations; operates ~6am–1:30am (2am Fri/Sat)
Bus Run by EMT (Empresa Municipal de Transportes); covers gaps in metro coverage; A/C, wheelchair accessible
Taxi Widely available, metered, government-regulated fares; good for late night/hard-to-reach spots
Walking Very pedestrian-friendly; Puerta del Sol, Plaza Mayor, Retiro Park all walkable from each other
Cycling Growing bike lane infrastructure; rental services available

Bonus: Madrid Cable Car (Teleférico)

  • ⚠️ CLOSED FOR RENOVATIONS UNTIL 2026 — do not sell/recommend currently
  • Connects Parque del Oeste and Casa de Campo
  • Spans ~2.5 km (1.5 mi)
  • Views include Royal Palace, Almudena Cathedral, Manzanares River

Brief History (exam-likely — sequence of eras)

  1. Foundation — 9th century: Established as a Moorish fortress, originally named "Mayrit"; served as a strategic point between Toledo and Segovia
  2. Christian Reconquest — 11th–12th century
  3. Golden Age / Imperial Capital — 16th–17th century
  4. Modernization and Capital Status — 19th–20th century

Climate & Best Time to Visit

  • Predominantly dry climate, minimal rain/snow year-round — a viable year-round destination
  • Summer: crowded with tourists; locals head to the coast to escape heat
  • Spring & Autumn: mild temps + lower accommodation prices → ideal time to visit (exam-likely recommendation)

Key Attractions

Prado MuseumTap to flip
Prado MuseumPRAH-doh myoo-ZEE-um
Golden Triangle of Art

Spain's largest and most-visited museum — over 7,000 paintings in the collection, though only ~1,500 are on display at once. Home to Velázquez, Goya, and other Spanish masters, plus Flemish works by Rubens and Van Dyck.

Learn more
Royal PalaceTap to flip
Royal Palace
Europe's largest

135,000 sq meters and 3,418 rooms — the largest royal palace in Europe. Built in 1764 to replace the Alcázar, which burned down decades earlier. Nearly the whole palace, including the Armoury, is open to visitors.

Learn more
Plaza MayorTap to flip
Plaza MayorPLAH-sah mah-YOR
Est. 16th century

Dates to the late 1500s, originally named Plaza del Arrabal. Centerpiece: an equestrian statue of King Philip III. Nine entrances lead into the square, the most famous being El Arco de Cuchilleros.

Learn more

Prado Museum (Museo Nacional del Prado)

  • Over 7,000 paintings in the collection; only ~1,500 on display at a time (exam-likely numbers)
  • Established ~200 years ago
  • Key artists: Spanish masters Velázquez and Goya; Flemish masters Rubens, Bruegel, Van Dyck
  • Address: Calle de Ruiz de Alarcón 23, Madrid
  • Hours: Mon–Sat 10am–8pm, Sun 10am–7pm

Plaza Mayor

  • Dates to late 16th century; originally named Plaza del Arrabal — hosted the city's main market
  • Centerpiece: equestrian statue of King Philip III — sculpted by Giambologna, finished by Pietro Tacca (1616); moved here from Casa de Campo in 1848 by Queen Isabella II (exam-likely dates)
  • Casa de la Panadería (est. 1590) — originally the city's most important bakery; now houses the Tourist Info Centre + artisan gift shop
  • El Arco de Cuchilleros — most famous of the plaza's nine entrances
  • Annual events: Easter drum parade, outdoor concerts, December Christmas market

El Retiro Park

  • Formerly royal-only; opened to the public in the late 19th century
  • 350 acres — called "the lungs of Madrid"
  • Activities: running, cycling, skating, rowboats on the Estanque, horse-drawn carriage rides
  • Landmarks: Velázquez Palace, Crystal Palace, statue of the Fallen Angel (only sculpture in the world depicting Lucifer — exam-likely fact), Puppet Theater (unique in Europe)
  • Hours: Daily 6am–10pm

Royal Palace of Madrid (Palacio Real)

  • Europe's largest royal palace — 135,000 sq meters, 3,418 rooms (exam-likely numbers)
  • Built 1764, replacing the Alcázar castle (destroyed by fire ~3 decades prior)
  • Nearly all open to the public, including the Armoury and Pharmacy

San Miguel Market (Mercado de San Miguel)

  • Near Plaza Mayor; major culinary hotspot in Europe
  • Known for wine, cheese, ham, cured meats, tapas
  • Hours: Sun–Thu 10am–midnight, Fri/Sat 10am–1am
  • Website: mercadodesanmiguel.es/en

Paseo del Arte (Art Walk)

  • Madrid's three major art galleries — Prado, Reina Sofía, and Thyssen-Bornemisza — sit within a short walk of each other, forming the "Golden Triangle of Art" (full artist breakdown for each museum in Section “TOP SITES BY LOCALE (Job Aid)”, Top Sites → Madrid)
  • Ticket validity: 1 year, allowing repeat visits

Faro de Moncloa (Moncloa's Lighthouse)

  • Former transmission tower, 92 meters tall; panoramic views up to ~100 km on a clear day
  • Max stay at top: 30 minutes
  • Hours: Daily 9:30am–8pm
  • May close in bad weather

Teatro Lara

  • Small 19th-century theatre; comedies, children's shows, musical acts
  • Advance booking recommended

Bonus: Temple of Debod (Templo de Debod)

  • Ancient Egyptian temple, located in Parque del Oeste
  • Dates to 2nd century BC; originally in the Nile Valley, dismantled and reconstructed in Madrid
  • Donated by Egypt in 1968 as thanks for Spain's help preserving the Abu Simbel temples
  • One of the few Egyptian temples outside Egypt — lesser-known, often overlooked by tourists

Destination Distance from Madrid Travel Time Round-Trip Train Cost
Toledo ~70 km (43 mi) south ~30 min–1 hr ~€20 (bus ~€10–15)
Segovia ~90 km (56 mi) northwest ~1–1.5 hrs ~€20 (bus similar)

*Source material refers to this site as "Valle de Colgamuros" in body text, though the lesson title says "Valle de los Caídos" — this valley was officially renamed Valle de Cuelgamuros in recent years. Worth confirming current official name for the exam.

Toledo

  • UNESCO World Heritage Site; known as the "City of Three Cultures" — historical coexistence of Christian, Jewish, and Muslim communities (exam-likely nickname)
  • Key sights: Alcázar fortress, Toledo Cathedral, old Jewish Quarter
  • Local specialty: marzipan sweets

Segovia

  • UNESCO World Heritage Site
  • Known for: Roman aqueduct, fairy-tale castle, charming old town, Alcázar of Segovia (fortress-palace on a rocky outcrop)
  • Local specialty: cochinillo (suckling pig)

El Escorial & Valle de los Caídos

  • Royal Site of San Lorenzo de El Escorial — UNESCO World Heritage Site; serves as royal palace, monastery, and mausoleum (houses remains of several Spanish monarchs)
  • Valle de los Caídos — controversial monument built by Francisco Franco commemorating those who died in the Spanish Civil War
  • Entry fees to each site: typically €10–15

Events & Festivals in Madrid

Festival Timing Highlights
San Isidro Festival Mid-May, ~1 week Honors patron saint San Isidro Labrador; dances, processions, concerts, bullfights; pilgrimage to San Isidro's hermitage (traditional attire)
Madrid Pride (Orgullo Madrid) Late June–early July, ~1 week One of the largest LGBTQ+ pride festivals in the world; millions of attendees; parades, concerts, parties; culminates in the Pride Parade
Veranos de la Villa Late June–early September Summer cultural festival; music, dance, theater, art across multiple venues (incl. open-air concerts at Plaza Mayor)
Fiestas de la Paloma August Honors Virgen de la Paloma, patron saint of the La Latina neighborhood; street parties, procession, Verbena de la Paloma street fair

Restaurants, Cafés & Nightlife

Cultural context

  • Spanish proverb: "Pan, vino y carne… crían buena sangre" — "Bread, wine, and meat make good blood"
  • Madrid's food scene is a fusion of regional Spanish cuisines (Andalucía, Galicia, Asturias, etc.) rather than one single "Madrid" cuisine — some debate whether Madrid has its own distinct culinary identity
  • ⚠️ Client tip: always reserve a table in Madrid; dinner is typically not served before 8pm

High-End / Michelin Restaurants

Restaurant Notes Hours
DiverXO 📍 Chef Dabiz Muñoz; 12-course tasting menu, Asian-inspired/inventive Spanish cuisine (e.g., Iberian pork dumplings w/ gochujang, cuttlefish, mochi w/ tom kha kai) Tue–Fri 1–6:30pm / 7:30pm–12am; closed Sat–Sun
El Club Allard 📍 Opened to the public in 2003 (formerly a private club); 2 Michelin stars; inventive Spanish cuisine, elegant chandeliered dining room Tue–Sat 1:30–3:30pm / 8:30–11pm

Currency & Practical Money Tips

Currency

  • Official currency: Euro (EUR) — same across all of Spain
  • ATMs widely available; withdraw in euros via credit/debit card
  • Most shops, restaurants, hotels accept major credit cards

Credit Cards

  • Visa and MasterCard most widely accepted; American Express accepted but less commonly than Visa/MC
  • Recommend clients carry at least one major card
  • ⚠️ Client tip: notify credit card issuer of travel dates/destination before departure to avoid fraud flags

Exchange Rates & Payment

  • Check exchange rates before travel; favorable-rate cards can help
  • Some smaller shops/markets are cash-only — advise carrying some euros
  • Currency conversion fees may apply — advise choosing payment method carefully
  • Be aware of ATM withdrawal fees (both from the ATM operator and the client's own bank)

Tipping (exam-likely — percentages) - Not obligatory in Spain — service charge is often already included in the bill - Customary: round up the bill or leave 5–10% in restaurants/bars/cafés - Larger tip common in formal dining, especially for exceptional service - Taxi drivers: rounding up the fare is appreciated, not required

Culture & Etiquette

Siesta & Late-Night Culture

  • Siesta = midday rest during the hottest part of the day; smaller/family-run businesses may close for a few hours in the afternoon (large chains usually stay open)
  • Dinners start later than in many countries; locals often dine as late as 8pm, then go out to bars/clubs afterward

Bullfighting (exam-likely — dates) - Tradition dates to the 18th century, when Plaza Mayor served as the city's original bullring - Las Ventas Bullring inaugurated 1931 — solidified Madrid as a central hub for bullfighting - Controversial: viewed by some as art (athleticism, grace, bravery), by others as an ethical concern — good to be aware of both perspectives when discussing with clients

Tapas Culture

  • Origin story: covering drinks with small plates to keep out flies
  • Tapas crawling = hopping bar to bar sampling small dishes
  • Classic tapas: patatas bravas (fried potatoes, spicy tomato sauce, aioli), jamón ibérico (cured ham), gambas al ajillo (garlic shrimp)
  • Tapas bar etiquette: order a drink first (often comes with a complimentary tapa); additional tapas ordered separately; discarding toothpicks/napkins on the floor is customary — used by the bartender to count tapas consumed for the bill (exam-likely quirky fact)

Soccer (Fútbol)

  • Madrid is home to two major clubs:
  • Real Madrid — plays at Santiago Bernabéu Stadium; fans called "Madridistas"
  • Atlético de Madrid — plays at Wanda Metropolitano Stadium
  • Their rivalry = the "Madrid Derby", dating back to the early 20th century — one of the fiercest rivalries in world football

General Etiquette

Topic Key Points
Greetings Handshake in formal/business settings; friends/acquaintances often kiss on each cheek, starting with the right cheek; wait for the other person to initiate in professional settings
Mealtimes Lunch ~1:30–3:30pm; dinner ~8:30pm or later; many restaurants closed outside these windows
Siesta hours Roughly 2–5pm; avoid loud/disruptive activity out of respect for those resting
Dress code Smart-casual recommended, especially evenings; avoid flip-flops/beachwear at religious sites, fine dining, cultural events
Language English widely spoken, but attempting Spanish is appreciated; polite phrase to ask: "¿Habla usted inglés?" (Do you speak English?)

Common Spanish Phrases

Phrase Pronunciation Meaning
Hola OH-lah Hello
Gracias GRAH-syas Thank you
Por favor por fah-VOHR Please
¿Cómo estás? KOH-moh ehs-TAHS How are you?
Me gusta meh GOO-stah I like it
Adiós ah-dee-OHS Goodbye

Traveler-Specific Notes

  • LGBTQ+: Madrid is one of Europe's most LGBTQ-friendly cities; scene centers on Chueca; hosts one of the world's largest Pride festivals (ties to earlier Madrid Pride festival notes)
  • Solo Female Travelers: generally considered safe/welcoming; well-lit areas, efficient public transit; female-only dorm options available at some accommodations; standard common-sense precautions still advised
  • Traveling with Children: family-friendly attractions include Retiro Park (boat rides, puppet show), CosmoCaixa Science Museum, Madrid Zoo Aquarium; pedestrian-friendly streets support family travel

Insider Travel Tips (for client differentiation)

  • Go beyond the city center: Lavapiés, Malasaña, and Chamberí offer street art, boutiques, and local cafés away from tourist crowds
  • Free museum hours: the Golden Triangle museums (Prado, Reina Sofía, Thyssen-Bornemisza) offer free admission during specific hours on certain days — good value-add tip for clients
  • Mercado de San Miguel off-peak: visit early morning or late evening to avoid crowds
  • Off-the-beaten-path flamenco: smaller local tablaos/cultural centers offer a more intimate experience than the big-name venues
  • BiciMAD: Madrid's public bike share system; stations throughout the city center and along the Manzanares River — good eco-friendly option for short trips

🎨 BARCELONA

Tap to flip
bar-suh-LOH-nuh

Passport & visa requirements are the same as the rest of Spain — see Section “PASSPORT & VISA INFORMATION” above.

Overview

  • Second-largest city in Spain
  • Spain's #1 tourist destination — ahead of Madrid (exam-likely fact)
  • Sunny/beautiful weather ~8 months per year

Origins & Identity

  • Founded by the Romans, originally named Barcino (1st century BC)
  • Original settlement located where today's cathedral stands; overshadowed at the time by Tarragona (provincial capital)
  • Visigoths and Moors also invaded, but had less lasting influence than the Franks, who arrived in the late 9th century — this is when Barcelona/Catalonia began forming a distinct identity from the rest of Spain
  • Catalan is its own language, not a Spanish dialect — related to other Romance languages
  • Castilian (Spanish) has many Arabic-derived words
  • Catalan has many French-derived words instead
  • (exam-likely distinction — good to know when discussing local culture with clients)

Brief History (exam-likely — sequence of eras)

  1. Roman Foundation — 1st century BC: settlement named Barcino; defensive wall built (remnants still visible in the Gothic Quarter)
  2. Medieval and Gothic Period — 5th–15th century: Barcelona grew into a significant Mediterranean trading hub; the Gothic Quarter's architecture reflects this era's prosperity; city passed through Visigoth and Moorish rule before the Christian Reconquista in the 15th century
  3. Modern Era and Catalan Identity — 17th–20th century: Continued to flourish through the Renaissance; faced the War of Spanish Succession (early 18th century); became a hub of industrialization in the 19th/early 20th century alongside a surge in Catalan nationalism; played a crucial role in the Spanish Civil War (1936–1939); faced significant upheaval under Francisco Franco's dictatorship
  4. Post-Franco Renaissance — 20th century onward: After Franco's death in 1975, Spain transitioned to democracy and Barcelona underwent a cultural/economic renaissance; hosted the 1992 Summer Olympics, driving major urban development and international attention (exam-likely date); has since grown into a major global tourist destination known for unique architecture, vibrant culture, and strong Catalan identity

(Full neighborhood breakdown consolidated below — see Key Neighborhoods table later in this section.)

Climate & Best Time to Visit

  • Summer (July–August): hottest, most crowded; temps up to 37°C; nearby beaches popular but busy
  • Spring & Autumn: best time to visit — good weather, fewer crowds, more affordable prices, easier restaurant/hotel availability (mirrors Madrid's seasonal recommendation)
  • Winter: mild, cool — no negative temps/frost, still explorable

Airport (exam-likely — official name & key facts)

  • Official name: Josep Tarradellas Barcelona–El Prat Airport (aka Barcelona Airport / El Prat Airport)
  • Location: 13 km southwest of city center
  • Address: Aeropuerto Josep Tarradellas Barcelona-El Prat
  • Website: aena.es/en/josep-tarradellas-barcelona-el-prat.html
  • Two terminals:
  • T1 — inaugurated 2009; primary terminal for domestic & international flights
  • T2 — divided into 3 sections (A, B, C); mainly low-cost/charter airlines
  • Free shuttle bus between T1 and T2, ~10 minutes
  • Facilities: shops, restaurants, lounges, car rental, currency exchange, taxis, buses, dedicated train service

Airport → City Center Options

Option Details
Aerobús Serves both terminals every 5 min; stops at Plaça Espanya, Plaça Universitat, Plaça Catalunya; ~25 min; one-way €5.90 / round-trip €10.20
Train From station next to Terminal 2; departs every 30 min; ~30 min to Sants Station; ticket €4
Taxi Available just outside terminals; price varies by traffic, luggage, day/time

Getting Around Barcelona

Mode Key Facts
Metro Easiest way to see main sights; runs 5am–midnight weekdays, until 2am or all night weekends/holidays; single ticket or multi-day pass (also valid for bus/tram)
Bus Covers entire city; runs all night — good for late-night transport; same ticket as metro, or hop-on/hop-off tourist bus ticket; dedicated bus lanes
Taxi Reasonably priced; taxi stands or hail on street; MyTaxi app for booking; most accept cards but confirm first, carry some cash as backup
Tram 6 lines; connects to suburbs/nearby cities (L'Hospitalet, Badalona); links with metro/bus; same ticket valid
Cycling 200 km (124 mi) of bike lanes; rental shops or Bicing public bike-share (400+ stations)

Bonus: Cable Car (Telefèric de Montjuïc)

  • Panoramic views of Barcelona, the Mediterranean, and iconic landmarks
  • Departs from Port Vell (near Barceloneta Beach) → Montjuïc Hill castle, ~10 minutes
  • ⚠️ Not ideal for clients with a fear of heights

Architecture Overview

  • Known globally for a unique blend of historical & modern styles, use of light/color, and emphasis on functionality/innovation
  • Catalan Modernism (Art Nouveau): developed late 19th–early 20th century; organic forms, intricate decoration, bold color/light — best known through Antoni Gaudí's work (Sagrada Família, La Pedrera, Park Güell); also seen in the former Hospital de Sant Pau
  • Other notable modern architecture: Norman Foster's Torre de Collserola, Calatrava's Torre Telefónica

Park Güell

  • Public park/garden with architectural elements in the Gràcia district; hilltop views over the city
  • Entirely designed by Gaudí; statues/buildings in varied colors and shapes
  • UNESCO World Heritage Site
  • Address: Carrer d'Olot, Barcelona | Hours: Daily 9:30am–7:30pm | Phone: +34 934 09 18 31 | Email: parkguell@bsmsa.cat

Basílica de Santa Maria del Mar

  • Considered the best existing example of Catalonian Gothic — cleaner style than typical Gothic
  • Built 1329–1383 — notably fast construction for the era (exam-likely dates)
  • Features: three naves of equal height, slender pillars, sparse chapel decoration, rose window + stained glass
  • Address: Plaça de Santa Maria 1, Barcelona (near the Picasso Museum) | Hours: Mon–Sat 9am–1pm/5–8:30pm, Sun 10am–2pm/5–8pm | Phone: +34 933 10 23 90

La Sagrada Família

  • Gaudí's unfinished masterpiece — remains incomplete to this day; still receives ~4.5 million visitors/year (exam-likely number)
  • Considered the best example of Modernist architecture; large unfinished Roman Catholic minor basilica
  • Guided/audio tours available in several languages
  • Address: Carrer de Mallorca 401 | Hours: Daily 9am–6pm | Metro: Sagrada Familia (lines 2, 5) | Phone: +34 932 08 04 14 | Email: informacio@sagradafamilia.org

Casa Batlló

  • Gaudí's renovation of a previously unremarkable building on Passeig de Gràcia; striking, almost beast-like exterior; twisted, idiosyncratic interior
  • Address: Passeig de Gràcia 43 | Hours: Daily 9am–8pm | Phone: +34 932 16 03 06 | Email: info@casabatllo.cat

Casa Milà (La Pedrera)

  • Built 1906–1912; nicknamed "La Pedrera" ("The Stone Quarry"); Gaudí's last private residence design (exam-likely fact)
  • Wrought-iron/stone-carved façade; striking interior, incl. rooms showing how residents actually lived
  • Address: Passeig de Gràcia 92 | Hours: Mon–Wed 9am–6:30pm; Thu–Sun 9am–6:30pm/9–11pm | Phone: +34 932 14 25 76 | Email: web@fcatalunyalapedrera.com

Cathedral of Barcelona (Cathedral of the Holy Cross and Santa Eulàlia) - Gothic cathedral, seat of the Archbishop of Barcelona - Construction began 1298, built on an ancient Roman temple site; took 150+ years to complete - Located in the Gothic Quarter; dedicated to Santa Eulàlia (patron saint of Barcelona), whose remains are buried under the main altar - Courtyard features 13 white geese — representing Saint Eulàlia's age at martyrdom (exam-likely quirky fact) - Rooftop accessible for city views - Address: Pla de la Seu s/n | Hours: Mon–Fri 8am–12:45pm/1–5:30pm/5:45–7:30pm; Sat 8am–12:45pm/1–5pm/5:15–8pm; Sun 8am–1:45pm/2–5pm/5:15–8pm | Metro: Jaume I | Phone: +34 933 15 15 54 | Website: catedralbcn.org | Email: info@catedralbcn.org

  • 360° city views; located in the Carmel neighborhood, atop Rovira

Events & Festivals in Barcelona

Dates/details vary year to year — confirm current info before finalizing client trip dates

Festival Timing Highlights

Restaurants, Cafés & Nightlife

Cultural context

  • Same Spanish proverb as Madrid: "Pan, vino y carne… crían buena sangre" — "Bread, wine, and meat make good blood"
  • Barcelona's food scene splits broadly into "the new" (modern/innovative — incl. famed chef Ferrán Adrià) and "the old" (traditional Catalan)
  • Traditional Catalan vegetable dishes: samfaina (a ratatouille), escalivada (grilled peppers/aubergine/onion), espinacs a la Catalana (spinach with garlic, pine nuts, raisins)
  • Simplest classic: pa amb tomàquet — bread with olive oil, salt, crushed tomato
  • "New" restaurants tend to be pricier; many chefs' apprentices have opened more affordable spots; "old" restaurants generally better value (though still not cheap)
  • ⚠️ Client tip: always reserve; dinner not served until 9pm (later than Madrid's 8pm)

Key Neighborhoods

Neighborhood Character
Barri Gòtic (Gothic Quarter) One of the oldest areas, near the sea; shopping enclave; Roman wall remnants visible (see Origins & Identity above)
El Raval Across La Rambla from Barri Gòtic; historically a slum area (until the 1980s), home to the city's Chinatown (Barrio Chino) and former red-light district; now gentrified with designer shops/cafés
Eixample Created by the 19th-century city expansion; wide avenues, upscale atmosphere; vast district with iconic Modernist architecture, incl. Passeig de Gràcia, Casa Batlló, La Pedrera
Gràcia Lively, bohemian; narrow streets, charming squares, vibrant cultural scene; popular with artists and young professionals (note: Park Güell is located within this district)
El Born (La Ribera) Between the Gothic Quarter and Barceloneta; trendy historic district; medieval streets, fashionable boutiques; mix of history and contemporary urban living (home to Dr Stravinsky bar, near Santa Maria del Mar)

Note: Gràcia is home to Park Güell; El Born is home to Dr Stravinsky bar and sits near Santa Maria del Mar.

Currency & Tipping

Same as Madrid/rest of Spain — Euro (EUR), Visa/MasterCard widely accepted, notify card issuer before travel, some cash-only spots exist. See Section “MADRID” (Madrid → Currency & Practical Money Tips) for full detail. - Tipping in Barcelona: round up the bill, or tip ~5–10% if service charge isn't already included — same guidance as Madrid

Culture & Etiquette

Overview

  • Blends Catalonian tradition with modern influences — architecture, arts, sports, culinary scene (traditional Catalan + innovative)
  • Notable quote: architect Charles-Édouard Jeanneret (Le Corbusier) praised Barcelona as "a city full of life, intense, a port open to the past and future"

Siesta

  • Same tradition as Madrid — midday rest during the hottest part of the day; some businesses close, though less consistently observed in urban/cosmopolitan areas of Barcelona specifically

Sports Culture (exam-likely — founding date, legends, dates) - FC Barcelona — founded 1899 (exam-likely date); plays at Camp Nou; legends include Johan Cruyff and Lionel Messi; numerous La Liga & UEFA Champions League titles - FC Barcelona Basket — competes in Liga ACB & EuroLeague; home arena: Palau Blaugrana - 1992 Olympic Games: held July 25–August 9; the 22nd modern Olympic Games; considered one of the most successful modern Olympics (ties to Olympic Park Montjuïc content above)

General Etiquette

Topic Key Points
Greetings Handshake typical; close friends/family may kiss both cheeks; use "Señor"/"Señora" titles unless invited to use first names
Mealtimes Lunch ~2:00pm; dinner ~9:00pm or later (consistent with the earlier note that Barcelona dinner starts later than Madrid's ~8pm); customary to linger after the meal
Siesta hours ~2–5pm
Cultural sensitivity Recognize distinct Catalan identity — avoid generalizing Catalonia as simply "Spain"
Dress code Smart dress in formal settings; beachwear fine at the beach only — cover up elsewhere
Language English widely spoken, but Catalan and Spanish both used locally — effort appreciated

Common Spanish Phrases (Same phrase set as Madrid — Hola, Gracias, Por favor, ¿Cómo estás?, Me gusta, Adiós — see Madrid Culture & Etiquette section for pronunciation table)

Traveler-Specific Notes

  • LGBTQ+: Spain broadly LGBTQ+-friendly; legalized same-sex marriage in 2005 — one of the earliest countries to do so (exam-likely date)
  • Solo Female Travelers: Spain has a low crime rate; standard precautions apply (secure belongings/crossbody bags in crowded areas, well-lit areas at night, know emergency numbers, dress modestly at religious sites)
  • Traveling with Children: family-friendly; public transit is accessible for families; kid-friendly attractions include Park Güell, Barcelona Zoo, Magic Fountain of Montjuïc, CosmoCaixa Science Museum

Insider Travel Tips (for client differentiation)

  • Bunkers del Carmel for sunset views: panoramic city views, less crowded than typical viewpoints (confirms/matches "The Bunker" noted earlier in Attractions section — same spot)
  • El Raval's hidden gems: explore beyond the main streets for less touristy cafés, boutiques, street art
  • Mercat dels Encants flea market: reiterated here as a top off-the-beaten-path shopping pick — near Glòries (see Shopping section above for full details: 14th-century origins, hours, etc.)
  • Secret gardens: Jardins de Rubió i Lluch, gardens at Palau Robert — quiet escapes from the busy city
  • Museu Can Framis: contemporary Catalan art museum in Poblenou — alternative to the (more famous, more crowded) Picasso Museum

🌊 VALENCIA

Tap to flip
bah-LEN-see-ah

Overview

  • Spain's 3rd largest city
  • Positioned as an uncrowded, authentic alternative to Barcelona/Madrid — the "real Spain"
  • European Green Capital 2024 — sustainability leader (green transport, waste management, urban green space)

Airport & Getting Around

  • Valencia Airport (VLC) — ~8 km west of the city center, ~20 min by taxi/transfer; metro line also connects airport to downtown
  • Compact, walkable historic center; the Turia Gardens (a former riverbed converted to a 9 km park) function as a natural walking/cycling spine connecting the old town to the City of Arts and Sciences
  • Valencia's bike-share and tram network are considered some of the best in Spain — ties to its Green Capital 2024 status
  • Well connected by AVE high-speed train to Madrid (~1.75 hrs) and Barcelona (~3 hrs)

History (exam-likely — founding date)

  • Roman origins: 138 BC
  • Later layered influences: Moors, Gothic, Renaissance periods

Key Landmarks / Architecture

La Lonja de la SedaTap to flip
La Lonja de la Sedalah LOHN-hah deh lah SEH-dah
UNESCO Site

UNESCO World Heritage Site — symbol of medieval economic power during Valencia's silk trade era, with intricate vaulted ceilings.

Learn more

Valencia Cathedral
Home of the Holy Grail

Blends Romanesque, Gothic, and Baroque styles; said to house the Holy Grail.

Learn more

City of Arts and Sciences

Learn more
Landmark Notes
La Lonja de la Seda (Silk Exchange) UNESCO World Heritage Site; symbol of medieval economic power; intricate vaulted ceilings
Valencia Cathedral Blends Romanesque, Gothic, Baroque styles; said to house the Holy Grail
Mercado Central Modernist architecture — stained glass, ironwork; also a working market

Food & Gastronomy

  • Paella originated in Valencia (exam-likely fact) — the original recipe uses rabbit, chicken, and snails, not seafood (that's a coastal adaptation better known abroad); order "paella valenciana" for the traditional version, "paella de marisco" for the seafood version tourists usually expect
  • Other local specialties: fresh seafood, citrus fruits (Valencia oranges are internationally famous), horchata (a chilled tiger-nut drink, distinct from the Mexican rice-based version), agua de Valencia (a local cava/orange juice cocktail, worth mentioning to clients looking for a "local" drink)
  • Notable food/dining spots: Mercado Central (one of Europe's largest fresh markets, great for a guided food tour), beachside restaurants at Malvarrosa and Las Arenas
  • 💡 Client-differentiating tip: since paella is Valencia's dish, cooking classes here carry more authenticity than the same experience in Madrid or Barcelona — worth highlighting to food-focused clients

Modern Attractions

  • City of Arts and Sciences — futuristic complex; includes the Oceanogràfic and an interactive science museum
  • Turia Gardens — ~9 km park built in a former riverbed; walking/cycling/picnicking; centerpiece of Valencia's sustainability story
  • El Carmen — historic district with lively atmosphere

Festivals / Culture

  • Las Fallas — UNESCO-recognized festival; art, satire, and fire, held in spring
  • Semana Santa Marinera (Holy Week) also referenced

Sustainability (tie to Green Capital 2024 status)

  • Extensive bike lanes, efficient public transit, pedestrian-friendly planning
  • Water conservation and waste reduction strategies
  • Turia Riverbed-to-park transformation cited as a model of urban planning

Partner / Booking Contact

  • Website: www.visitvalencia.com
  • Contact: Eva.Fernandez@visitvalencia.com
  • Positioned as a resource for itinerary planning support (Visit Valencia partner desk)

🧳 FAM Trip Notes (Aug 2025)

First-hand notes from a Kensington DE site visit.

  • Palau del Mar — Boutique Luxe, 67 rooms, 500m from the historic center in the Eixample district near the Turia Gardens. Two refurbished 19th-century stately homes with rooms oriented around quiet central courtyards; spa and indoor pool. Family rooms available (Deluxe is the third room category, after Dreamers and Superior, for smaller families). ⚠️ Small common areas; a new inner patio was still being finished as of this visit — worth confirming it's complete before quoting.
  • Westin Valencia — Luxe, 135 rooms and suites, Art Deco building in a peaceful upscale neighborhood a short walk from the Old Town (~15 min). Westin's signature "Heavenly Beds," a strong spa, and a serene inner courtyard garden. Connecting rooms/suites for families, max 3 pax per room.
  • Hotel Puerta Serranos (listed 4★ here vs. Premier in the FAIR note above — consistent) — contemporary design, boutique ambience; one of several solid Valencia options alongside MYR Palacio Vallier and Caro Hotel (see Tommie's Hotels above for Caro).

New Valencia tour worth knowing: San José Caves (4 hrs, hotel pickup with driver/guide, entrance fees included) — 45 minutes north of Valencia. The largest navigable underground river in Europe (3 km long, up to 11m deep, source still unknown). Walking sections plus a small boat ride (max 10 pax) with an English-speaking skipper-guide. Water is a cool 17°C; expect a ~30-min wait on arrival and about an hour for the visit; photography only allowed briefly at the end. Elevate with a paella lunch nearby, the shoe museum, the rice fields, or after-hours kayak tours. Best for nature lovers and families — flag the accessibility caveat: uneven surfaces, steps, narrow passages, and boat access that can be tricky for reduced mobility.

💃 SEVILLE 🏛️

Tap to flip
seh-VEE-yah

Andalusia's capital and the most-visited city in the region. Full site/tour/hotel detail already lives in the Job Aid tables (Sections 1.6–1.10) — this section adds the orientation and framing those tables don't cover.

Why clients love it: Seville is the "quintessential Andalusia" stop — flamenco, tapas culture, Mudéjar/Gothic architecture, and the Guadalquivir River running through the historic center. It's flatter and more walkable than Granada, with a livelier nightlife scene than Córdoba.

Getting there: Seville Airport (SVQ), ~10 km from the city center, ~15–20 min by taxi/transfer. Also reachable via AVE high-speed train from Madrid (~2.5 hrs) or Córdoba (~45 min) — see Section “ARRIVALS & TRANSFERS (Job Aid)” for general train booking rules.

Orientation — key neighborhoods: | Neighborhood | Character | |---|---| | Santa Cruz | Historic Jewish Quarter; cobblestone streets, tapas bars, orange trees; home to the Cathedral & Royal Alcázar (see Section “POPULAR HOTELS BY LOCALE (Job Aid)” for hotel picks here) | | El Centro | Bustling commercial core beside Santa Cruz; more family-friendly, less charming | | Triana | Across the river; considered the birthplace of flamenco and home to authentic, less touristy tapas bars — worth mentioning to clients seeking a "locals" experience beyond Santa Cruz |

Signature sites (full detail in Section “TOP SITES BY LOCALE (Job Aid)”): Seville Cathedral (largest Gothic cathedral in the world) and the Royal Alcázar (one of Europe's oldest royal palaces still in use) — both featured on the flip-cards above. ⚠️ Confirmed via live Kensington itineraries: passports are required to visit the Royal Alcázar, and failure to present one may result in denied access.

Best time to visit: March–May and September–November (see Section “WEATHER BY LOCALE” Weather for exact temperatures) — avoid July/August unless the client genuinely tolerates extreme heat (regularly 40°C+/104°F+).

💡 Client-differentiating tips: - Seville hosts two of Spain's most famous festivals: Semana Santa (Holy Week, March/April) and the Feria de Abril (April Fair, ~2 weeks after Easter) — hotel prices spike and book out early for both - Flamenco here is considered more "authentic" than in Madrid by purists, since Andalusia (and Triana specifically) is where the art form originated

Alfonso XIII
Luxe

🔍 FAIR inspection (Oct 2023): confirms Luxe — no conflict. Commissioned by the King in the 1920s; guests have included Princess Diana and Elton John; the building itself is government-owned, a protected monument. Triple occupancy from Deluxe/Grande Deluxe up; suites connect to Grande Deluxe, Executive to Deluxe, Deluxe to Deluxe. Sauna on-site; last full refurbishment 2012. Buffet breakfast 7–11am.

🏰 GRANADA 🏔️

Tap to flip
grah-NAH-dah

Home to the Alhambra — one of Spain's two single most-visited sites (alongside Sagrada Família) — and the last Moorish stronghold in Spain.

Why clients love it: Granada blends Moorish, Christian, and Sierra Nevada mountain influences into one city — the Alhambra alone justifies the stop, and the Albaicín's winding streets offer some of the most romantic viewpoints in Spain (especially at sunset, looking back at the Alhambra).

Getting there: Federico García Lorca Granada-Jaén Airport (GRX), ~15 km from the city, limited direct international routes (many clients connect via Madrid or Barcelona). AVE train from Madrid takes ~3.25 hrs; regional train/bus from Seville ~3 hrs.

Orientation: The historic center sits below the Alhambra hill; most preferred hotels are here (see Section “POPULAR HOTELS BY LOCALE (Job Aid)”), roughly 20 minutes by car/taxi to the Alhambra itself. The Albaicín (old Moorish quarter) and Sacromonte (traditional Roma cave-house district, known for flamenco "zambra" shows) are the two neighborhoods most worth a client's leisure time beyond the Alhambra.

Signature sites (full detail in Section “TOP SITES BY LOCALE (Job Aid)”): the Alhambra Palace (⚠️ passport required to book and to bring on visit day) and Granada Cathedral.

Best time to visit: April–May and September–October — see Section “WEATHER BY LOCALE” for exact figures. Granada's proximity to the Sierra Nevada means bigger day/night temperature swings than the coast, even in summer.

💡 Client-differentiating tips: - Alhambra tickets sell out months in advance during peak season — this is one of the most important "book early" conversations to have with a client - Granada is one of the last places in Spain with a genuine free tapa with every drink tradition — a fun, money-saving detail to share with budget-conscious clients

🧳 FAM Trip Notes (Aug 2025)

New tour from a Kensington DE site visit: Half Day Olive Oil Tour (with tasting & lunch, ~2 hrs on-site / can run up to 5 hrs total) — usually run from Granada; the mill is in Nigüelas in the Lecrín Valley, ~30 min away, at the foot of the Sierra Nevada. Visits La Erilla Oil Mill, the oldest working oil mill in Spain (dating to the 15th century). Guide walks through the full process — hand-harvesting through pressing (a 24-hour process) and animal-powered vs. mechanical extraction — then a tasting of three olive oil grades (regular, virgin, extra virgin) evaluated by sight, smell, and taste. Basic tapas lunch included (jamón, tortilla, Manchego). Harvest season is October–February. Ideal for foodies and clients interested in heritage; can be elevated with a proper sit-down lunch or a visit to the olive groves themselves. Short walk from parking to the mill; no major mobility flags noted.

🕌 CÓRDOBA 🔥

Tap to flip
KOR-doh-bah

Often the most overlooked of the Andalusian "golden triangle" cities, but home to the Mezquita — one of the most architecturally significant buildings in the Islamic world.

Why clients love it: Córdoba is smaller and quieter than Seville or Granada, with an intact Jewish Quarter (Judería), the famous Patios Festival (May), and a walkable historic center that can genuinely be seen in a day. It's most often sold as a day trip or a 1-night add-on rather than a multi-night stay (see Section “TOP ITINERARIES (Job Aid)” itinerary logic).

Getting there: Córdoba has no major commercial airport — nearly all visitors arrive by AVE high-speed train, most commonly from Madrid (~1.75 hrs) or Seville (~45 min). This is an important detail for advisors: don't plan flight logistics into Córdoba, only rail or private transfer.

Orientation: The Judería (Jewish Quarter) surrounds the Mezquita and is the historic core most clients will walk through; it's compact enough that most preferred hotels (Section “POPULAR HOTELS BY LOCALE (Job Aid)”) are within a 10–15 minute walk of everything.

Signature sites (full detail in Section “TOP SITES BY LOCALE (Job Aid)”): the Mosque-Cathedral (Mezquita), Medina Azahara (a 10th-century caliphate city just outside town — ⚠️ closed Sunday PM & Monday), and the Alcázar de los Reyes Cristianos.

Best time to visit: March–May and October — see Section “WEATHER BY LOCALE” for exact figures. Córdoba and Seville constantly trade the title of "hottest city in Europe" — July/August highs regularly exceed 40°C (104°F).

💡 Client-differentiating tips: - If a client's itinerary is tight on nights, Córdoba is the easiest of the four Andalusian cities to convert into a day trip (from Seville or en route Seville→Granada) rather than an overnight — see Section “POPULAR HOTELS BY LOCALE (Job Aid)” for that framing - The Patios Festival (May) opens Córdoba's famously flower-filled private courtyards to the public — a wonderful, lesser-known event to mention to culture-focused clients traveling in that window

🏖️ MARBELLA 🏖️

Tap to flip
mar-BEH-yah

The Costa del Sol's most glamorous resort town — the "beach and relaxation" bookend most Spain Grand Tour-style itineraries end on (see Section “TOP ITINERARIES (Job Aid)”).

Why clients love it: Marbella is where clients decompress after a culture-heavy Spain itinerary — beaches, golf, marina glamour, and a completely different pace from Madrid/Andalusia's cities. It's been a jet-set destination since the 1960s.

Getting there: ⚠️ Marbella has no airport and no train station — every client arrives via Málaga-Costa del Sol Airport (AGP), ~50 km away (~35–40 min by car/private transfer). This is an important logistics note: always budget a private transfer from Málaga, not a train.

Orientation: | Area | Character | |---|---| | Old Town (Casco Antiguo) | Whitewashed streets, Plaza de los Naranjos, traditional tapas bars — the "authentic" side of Marbella | | Golden Mile | The stretch between Marbella and Puerto Banús — luxury villas, five-star resorts | | Puerto Banús | The marina made famous by superyachts and supercars; ~5 million visitors/year; can feel more like a spectacle than a destination, worth setting expectations |

Best time to visit: Given this is a beach/relaxation stop, summer (June–September) is actually the desired season here (unlike the cultural cities) — though spring/autumn are more comfortable and less crowded if the client's priority is golf or general leisure over beach time.

💡 Client-differentiating tips: - Alternatives with a similar beach/relaxation role but a different vibe: Málaga (more culture + beach blend, better for clients who still want some sightseeing) or Torremolinos/Fuengirola (more budget-friendly, family-oriented) — both already referenced in the Grand Tour of Spain itinerary notes (Section “TOP ITINERARIES (Job Aid)”) - Marbella pairs naturally with a Gibraltar or Ronda day trip for clients who want one more cultural excursion before flying home

Hotels — KT Preferred Properties

The Job Aid lists no preferred property; the live Grand Tour of Spain uses NH Collection Marbella (Discovery/Premier, 10 min walk to the beach). For Luxe clients the Golden Mile resorts (Puente Romano, Marbella Club) are the usual upgrade — confirm with the DMC.

💡 Anantara Villa Padierna Palace (Golden Mile) is a genuine third Luxe-tier option, not currently named elsewhere in this guide — 2026 rate (Kensington Contracted): from €256/night (Nov–Dec) up to €553–583/night (Jul–Aug peak), Deluxe Room, B&B. Kids under 13 stay free in an extra bed/crib, with complimentary Kids Club access. See Hotel Rate Reference.

🧳 FAM Trip Notes (Aug 2025)

First-hand notes from a Kensington DE site visit — richer color than the FAIR summary above for these three.

  • El Fuerte — Luxe, 250 rooms, best location in Marbella: on the beach but walking distance to the Old Town. Laid-back luxury, stylish and beachy rather than stuffy. No rooms explicitly labeled "family," but spacious suites and interconnecting rooms work well for families. Recently upgraded from 4★ to 5★. Selling points: packing/unpacking service, kids' club, a 10-step breakfast menu, nightly entertainment, Japanese toilets.
  • Amare Beach — Premier, adults-only, 236 rooms, beachfront in the heart of Marbella, steps from the Old Town. Chic and artsy. No family rooms or quads — but does have "keep the secret" triple rooms. Strong 4★ service level with concierge and push-button beach club service. Direct beach access, rooftop bar, daily DJ, included yoga classes.
  • Marbella Club — described as "Ultra Luxe," probably the best service level in Marbella. On the Golden Mile between the Old Town and Puerto Banús, beachfront, 10 acres of subtropical gardens. 131 rooms + 17 villas — genuinely strong for families (connecting rooms, suites, villas). One of Marbella's first beach clubs (1950s), Michelin-starred dining, all rooms ground/first floor (a real mobility plus), Montessori kids' club. ⚠️ Not walking distance to the Old Town or Puerto Banús — set that expectation up front.

Two more Marbella tours worth knowing, from the same FAM:

  • Half Day Tapas Tour (3 hrs) — a straightforward add-on for food-focused clients.
  • Half Day Nerja & Frigiliana Tour (5 hrs, the Axarquía region) — panoramic, no entrance fees included. Frigiliana is ~1.5 hrs east of Marbella; Nerja is 15 min further. Highlights: Frigiliana (one of the best examples of a classic white Andalusian village, cobbled streets, sea views) and "Europe's Balcony" viewpoint in Nerja (15-min photo stop). Can be elevated with the Nerja Caves (10 min away, 45-min visit) or the Maro waterfall — one of only two places in Spain where a river cascades directly into the sea, also good for kayaking. ⚠️ Frigiliana is steep — not ideal for clients with mobility concerns. Suitable for most other clients.

⚔️ TOLEDO ⚔️

Tap to flip
toh-LEH-doh

New section — Toledo, San Sebastián, and Bilbao are added here as full destinations rather than day-trip footnotes, since Kensington's own live itineraries sell Bilbao and San Sebastián as overnight stops, and Toledo genuinely rewards an overnight stay beyond the standard Madrid day trip.

Why clients love it: Toledo is the "City of Three Cultures" — Christian, Jewish, and Muslim heritage layered into one walled hilltop city on a bend of the River Tajo. It's Spain's medieval capital and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986. Most clients see it as a half-day trip from Madrid, but the city after dark — floodlit walls, empty cobbled streets, dinner on a rooftop overlooking the Alcázar — is a genuinely different (and better) experience than the day-trip crowds.

Getting there: High-speed AVE train from Madrid's Puerta de Atocha, ~30 minutes — the fastest, easiest connection in this entire guide. No airport; always route via Madrid.

Orientation: The historic center sits on a granite outcrop almost entirely encircled by the Tajo, so nearly everything is within a compact walkable core — steep in places (this is a hill city; flag for mobility concerns). Plaza de Zocodover is the natural landmark/meeting point at the center of the old town, a short walk from the Cathedral, the Alcázar, and the Jewish Quarter (Judería) that holds the Synagogue of Santa María la Blanca — Europe's oldest still-standing synagogue.

Best time to visit: Spring and autumn — the same logic as Madrid/inland Spain, since Toledo sits on the same continental plateau and can run hot and exposed in summer with little shade in the old town.

Signature sites: Toledo Cathedral (a 13th-century Gothic masterpiece, arguably second only to Seville's among Spain's cathedrals), the Alcázar of Toledo (a historic fortress, now home to the Army Museum), and the Monastery of San Juan de los Reyes. El Greco lived and worked here — the Museo del Greco and several of his paintings in situ (including in the Cathedral itself) are a real draw for art-focused clients. Local specialty: marzipan, sold throughout the old town, especially around convents that still bake it by hand.

🌊 SAN SEBASTIÁN 🌊

Tap to flip
sahn seh-bahs-tee-AHN

Why clients love it: San Sebastián (Donostia in Basque) has the highest concentration of Michelin stars per capita in the world, a Belle Époque waterfront wrapped around La Concha — widely considered one of Europe's most beautiful urban beaches — and a pintxos culture in the Old Town (Parte Vieja) that turns dinner into a bar-hopping event. It's the anchor of Kensington's Basque-region product (see "Barcelona to Bilbao: A Spanish Culinary Journey" and "A Taste of Bordeaux & Basque Region" in Live Website Listings) and pairs naturally with Bilbao.

Getting there: ⚠️ San Sebastián's own airport (EAS) is small with limited routes — most clients fly into Bilbao (BIO) and take a ~1-hour private transfer, or connect via Madrid/Barcelona. Direct high-speed rail is limited: Barcelona–San Sebastián by train runs ~6 hours, so a Bilbao flight + transfer is almost always the better routing (see the Common Domestic Flight Route Cheat Sheet in Section "Arrivals & Transfers").

Orientation: The city centers on La Concha bay, with the Old Town (Parte Vieja) at its eastern end — narrow streets packed with pintxos bars, and the departure point for a pintxos crawl (order a drink, take whatever's on the counter, move to the next bar). The Gros neighborhood, across the Urumea River, has a more local, surfer-beach feel (Zurriola beach) and is popular with younger/repeat clients. Monte Igueldo, at the western end of La Concha, has funicular views over the whole bay.

Best time to visit: Summer (June–September) is genuinely the best window here — this is a beach/coastal city, and the Basque coast stays milder than inland Spain even in August. The San Sebastián International Film Festival (mid-September) brings crowds and higher rates; flag this for clients with flexible dates.

Signature sites: La Concha beach and promenade, the Old Town's pintxos bars, Monte Igueldo's funicular and views, and — for food-focused clients — the sheer density of Michelin-starred dining. San Sebastián is as much a culinary destination as a sightseeing one; set that expectation with clients up front.

🐕 BILBAO 🐕

Tap to flip
beel-BAH-oh

Why clients love it: Bilbao is the Basque Country's largest city and the reason the "Bilbao Effect" entered urban-planning vocabulary — Frank Gehry's Guggenheim Museum Bilbao (1997) single-handedly transformed a declining industrial port city into a design/architecture destination. It pairs naturally with San Sebastián (~1 hour away) for a Basque-region product, and has its own strong, less internationally-hyped culinary scene.

Getting there: Bilbao Airport (BIO) has direct flights from Madrid, Barcelona, and several European hubs — this is the usual gateway for the whole Basque region, including San Sebastián (fly to Bilbao, then ~1-hour private transfer). Rail from Madrid runs ~5 hours on conventional lines — flight is almost always the better call given the 5-hour rule of thumb elsewhere in this guide.

Orientation: The Guggenheim sits on the Nervión/Ibaizabal estuary in the Abandoibarra district, a short walk from the Casco Viejo (Old Town) — the historic core, and the best pintxos-crawl territory in the city. The Ensanche (the 19th-century expansion district) has the main shopping street (Gran Vía) between the two.

Best time to visit: Similar logic to San Sebastián — summer is genuinely pleasant here (mild, coastal-influenced), though Bilbao doesn't have San Sebastián's beach-city July/August crowding, so it's a comfortable year-round city trip aside from winter rain.

Signature sites: The Guggenheim Museum Bilbao (Frank Gehry's titanium-clad landmark, plus Jeff Koons's "Puppy" sculpture out front), the Casco Viejo's Siete Calles (Seven Streets, the medieval core), and the Museo de Bellas Artes (fine arts museum, a serious collection often overlooked next to the Guggenheim's fame).

🌊 SPAIN — COSTA BRAVA & MEDITERRANEAN EXTENSION (FAM Notes, Aug 2025)

Source: Kensington FAM trip report, "From Costa del Sol to Costa Brava" (Spaintop, Aug 2025). This is genuinely new territory beyond the seven core locales covered elsewhere in this guide — Marbella, Granada, Murcia, Alicante, Valencia, Priorat, and Costa Brava, done as a single rental-car road trip along the Spanish Mediterranean coast. Useful for clients who want a coastal/road-trip alternative to the classic Madrid–Andalusia–Barcelona circuit, or an extension tacked onto either end of it.

Arrival/internal logistics: this itinerary is built around a rental car, not trains or private transfers between locales — a real difference from the core-city itinerary logic elsewhere in this guide, and worth flagging to clients who assumed a driver throughout.

Why Sell It (August / High Season)

AngleNotes
DifferentiationLess expensive than the French and Italian Rivieras; relatively unknown to North American clients; a less formal, less stylized vibe than those comparables
ClienteleClients who want the seaside as part of the trip and don't mind the heat — a mix of beach time, culture, food, and heritage
WeatherHot, sunny, dry in August — daytime highs ~30–35°C (86–95°F), minimal rainfall. Great for beach time, intense for sightseeing
Logistics & AccessibilityOvertourism in hotspots; long drives between locales; watch for heat waves and increasingly common jellyfish

Selling points to lead with: Blue Flag beaches with clean sand and strong facilities; scenic towns (Frigiliana, Pals, Calella); historic cities (Valencia, Girona); Mediterranean cuisine — tapas, paella, fresh seafood; summer festivals and moonlit fiestas (e.g. Feria de Málaga); a laid-back rhythm of long lunches, siesta, and late-night socializing.

Tours

  • Cartagena (Murcia) — Walking Tour (2–3 hrs)
  • Priorat — Full Day Wine Tour + Reus/Tarragona — winery visit (2–4 hrs) at Perinet, 30 min from Mas D'en Bruno, 2.5 hrs from Barcelona (overnight recommended). Priorat is a DOC region (alongside Rioja, the only two in Spain with that top-tier designation) — many medieval monasteries in the area, since monks introduced wine production here; harvest is difficult-access, by hand and donkey. Add-ons: Reus (Gaudí's birthplace, an Art Nouveau showcase — Casa Navas is a highlight) with vermouth tastings, plus Tarragona's old town and Roman amphitheater. Ideal for wine lovers exploring a lesser-known region, or anyone wanting to unplug. ⚠️ Twisty mountain roads — worth a heads-up for anyone prone to carsickness.
  • Costa Brava — Cooking Class at a Typical Masia (Country House) (3–3.5 hrs) — pickup at hotel, ~15 min from Mas d'en Torrent. A beautiful countryside masia using "km zero" produce; menu customizable (Catalan or Spanish focus) — sample menu: gazpacho, pa amb tomàquet, dorada fish, crema catalana, with meat options available. Check allergies in advance. Elevate with a market visit in a nearby town. Ideal for foodies and anyone interested in Catalan cuisine specifically.
  • Costa Brava — Full Day Girona & Costa Brava Villages Tour — a Girona walking tour (2–3 hrs) plus Pals and Calella, with a stop at the San Sebastián lighthouse; includes entry to Girona's Arab Baths (actually Christian-built, despite the name). Pals is a beautifully preserved medieval town (restored after the Civil War); Calella is a classic Mediterranean seaside village. A rice-fields stop ties into the region's paella culture — Spain is Europe's second-largest rice producer after Italy. Stops are customizable (Besalú, Tossa, Llafranch, Peratallada). ⚠️ Cadaqués is not recommended on this tour — hard to reach and requires arriving 30 min ahead for a Dalí House visit, which eats the day. Good for most clients and history buffs; especially interesting for Jewish heritage travelers (Girona + Besalú combo covers Girona's historic Jewish quarter). Pals itself has steps and steep streets — flag for mobility concerns. 💡 2026 marks the 100th anniversary of Gaudí's death — expect Sagrada Família and Park Güell tickets to get harder to secure.
  • Valencia — San José Caves — see the Valencia FAM notes above; same tour, applies here as an extension stop too.

🎟️ SPAIN — TOP TOURS BY LOCALE (Job Aid)

General Touring Considerations — Crowds, Tickets & Heat

Popularity of Top Sites

  • Sagrada Família, Alhambra, Prado Museum, and Park Güell each draw ~3 million visitors/year (exam-likely comparable figure — consistent with the earlier note that Sagrada Família alone sees 3M+ annually)

Crowds

  • Top sites and historic centers are busy year-round, especially peak season
  • Set client expectations upfront that sites will be busy
  • 💡 Sales angle: this is where KT's value shows — expert guides navigate crowds, private transfers keep the experience comfortable
  • ⚠️ Pre-purchased tickets with entry times do not mean skipping the line/security check — always set this expectation

Ticket Availability

  • Advance ticket sales are used to manage crowd size at top sites — this means tickets can sell out months ahead
  • Advise clients early on the importance of booking site tickets well in advance
  • 💡 For last-minute bookings where key sites are sold out: offer a walking tour viewing sites from the outside (many are stunning from exterior/lookout points), and book interior visits at less-busy alternative sites instead

Beating the Heat (exam-likely — July average temps by city) | City | July Average Temp Range | |---|---| | Madrid | 21–34°C (70–93°F) | | Seville | 21–37°C (70–99°F) | | Granada | 20–35°C (68–95°F) |

  • Heat can meaningfully affect client enjoyment — even pose safety risk if unprepared
  • Tips: remind clients about sun protection + hydration; book outdoor-site tours early morning or late afternoon; use car-based touring between sites (vs. walking) for heat relief

Tour Categories (framework used throughout this section)

  • First Visit Highlights: must-see sites for first-time visitors to a locale
  • Key Sites Deeper Dives: more in-depth — covers both popular and off-the-beaten-path sites
  • Hands-On / Participatory: experiential tours where clients learn or do a cultural activity led by a local

Each tour listing typically covers three angles: Description (incl. "wow" moments — useful phone-pitch material for clients), KT Value (why book with KT vs. visiting independently), and Key Alerts (expectations to manage / itinerary considerations).

KT Tour Levels

  • Most featured tours are Premier — Kensington's most popular Spain tour level; typically private, sometimes with car transfers to/from the touring spot
  • Price-conscious clients: small-group tour options also available in TMT
  • Luxe clients: Premier tours can be customized further — hot air balloon tours, helicopter tours, after-hours site visits, winery visits paired with a Michelin-starred restaurant (⚠️ these aren't in TMT yet — coming soon, so currently more manual to arrange)

(For pronunciation of Albaicín, Casa Batlló, Montserrat, Judería, Park Güell, and Alhambra, see the consolidated Pronunciation Guide in Section “PRONUNCIATION GUIDE” below.)

Madrid (Tour Category | KT Level noted per tour) - Recommended itinerary order: start in Madrid → Andalucía → end in Barcelona (lets Madrid "wow" before Barcelona, ends on the Mediterranean) - ½ Day Prado Museum & Royal Palace (First Visit Highlights | Premier) — 4 hrs w/ Liberty, 5 hrs w/ Spaintop; order depends on entrance tickets; can add Reina Sofía/Thyssen if client is an art lover; guides navigate crowds and bring the art/palace stories to life - ½ Day Toledo (First Visit Highlights | Premier) — 5 hrs, most popular day trip out of Madrid, UNESCO site; 1-hr drive to Toledo; a must for El Greco fans and those with Jewish heritage (Jewish/Catholic/Muslim coexistence theme); ⚠️ cobblestone streets challenging for mobility concerns; Liberty Spain includes Cathedral entrance, Spaintop does not; can extend to full day w/ marzipan tasting or winery visit - ½ Day Tapas Walking Tour (Hands-On/Participatory | Premier) — 3 hrs; visits 3 restaurants showcasing tapas culture; ⚠️ cannot accommodate vegans — share dietary restrictions in advance so guide can adapt; ⚠️ tour starts at set times: 1pm or 7pm — 7pm is recommended (more locals out in the evening)

Barcelona

  • ½ Day Gothic Quarter Walking Tour w/ Santa Maria del Mar & Sagrada Família (5 hrs) — entrance fees included; tour must start at proposed time (tickets); Sagrada tickets non-refundable & guaranteed only at purchase
  • ½ Day Cooking Class & Market Visit (4 hrs, w/ meal & wine) — at Boqueria Market; ⚠️ only available Tue–Sat mornings or Fri evening; not Mon; market closed Sun
  • ½ Day Gaudí's Barcelona (Casa Batlló, Casa Milà, Park Güell — 5 hrs) — admission included; little flexibility on start time; not mobility-friendly (steep ramps)
  • Montserrat Monastery & Winery (8 hrs w/ lunch) — combines monastery + Penedès region winery/cava tasting; morning pickup required to avoid crowds; ⚠️ avoid Saturdays/school holidays if client wants to see the boys' choir sing

Seville

  • ½ Day Walking Tour w/ Cathedral & Royal Alcázar (3 hrs) — entrance fees included; minimal walking (sites close together); clients must cover shoulders/mid-thigh + carry ID
  • Flamenco Show at El Arenal (1.5 hrs w/ drink, evening only) — pairs well with tapas tour or Cathedral/Alcázar tour; note: Corral de la Morería in Madrid is widely considered Spain's best flamenco show, though flamenco originates from Andalusia; no photos/videos, must stay silent during performance

Granada

  • ½ Day Alhambra Palace (2.5 hrs) — includes one-way taxi + entrance; private transport can't access Alhambra grounds directly (taxi allowed); best scheduled morning; after-hours option available
  • ½ Day Albaicín Quarter Walking Tour (5 hrs w/ lunch) — tasting menu w/ wine pairings; ⚠️ steep roads, not for mobility-limited clients; Spaintop uses 2 restaurants (Carmen El Agua, Las Tomasas), Liberty uses only Las Tomasas; guide drops clients at restaurant — return to hotel is on their own

Córdoba

  • ½ Day Medina Azahara (3 hrs) — lots of walking/steps, not for mobility-limited clients; closed Sun PM & Mon
  • ½ Day Monumental Walking Tour (3 hrs) — Mosque-Cathedral, Christian Monarchs' Alcázar, Synagogue entrance included; can add private Córdoba patio visit (esp. during May Patios Festival); if arriving by train from Seville, tour usually starts at the Alcázar (not train station)

🌦️ SPAIN — WEATHER BY LOCALE 🌦️

Spain runs on a Mediterranean/continental mashup: scorching, bone-dry summers almost everywhere, mild-to-cool winters, and the real "make or break" factor for comfort is simply how far inland a city sits. Coastal cities (Barcelona, Valencia) get a sea breeze that tempers the extremes; inland/plateau cities (Madrid, Seville, Córdoba, Granada) swing harder in both directions. Quick reads from the table (exam-likely — comparative facts):

  • Hottest in summer: Córdoba (37°C/99°F) — narrowly beats Seville (36°C/97°F); the two constantly trade the "hottest city in Europe" title
  • Coldest winter nights: Madrid and Granada tie at 2°C (36°F) — both are high-altitude/inland, away from the coast's moderating effect
  • Mildest overall: Barcelona — coastal location keeps both extremes in check
  • Universal rule of thumb: avoid Andalusia (Seville, Córdoba, Granada) in July–August unless your client genuinely loves heat; April–May and September–October are the sweet spot almost everywhere in Spain
  • ⚠️ Rain is a minor factor almost everywhere in Spain — even the "rainiest" months rarely wash out a trip; heat management matters far more than rain management for most of the year

🤝 DMCs IN SPAIN

Vendor/booking knowledge — Destination Management Companies (DMCs) operating in Spain

Module Learning Objectives

  1. Differentiate between the local DMCs and their areas of expertise
  2. Select the appropriate vendor for client scenarios

Overview

  • Kensington works with three local DMCs in Spain, each providing in-depth local knowledge/expertise
  • Spaintop and Liberty Spain — the two "core" DMCs providing Kensington's main Spain product
  • Family Twist — smaller, family-focused tour offering (supplementary, not core)

🧮 Quick Compare — Private Transfers (Airport/Train/Port)

Liberty Spain vs. Spaintop, side by side. Data pulled from each DMC's own 2026 tariff below — always confirm current rates in TMT before quoting.

Key Rule (exam-likely — booking logic)

  • ⚠️ You must select either Spaintop OR Liberty Spain as the core DMC for any Spain trip — they cannot be mixed
  • Family Twist can be added on top of either core DMC (Spaintop or Liberty Spain) if the client has family/kid-focused needs — it doesn't compete with the core product
  • Both core DMCs offer similar products and can often fulfill the same client request — balance business between both providers

Naming note: Spaintop was previously named DENIR — you may still see "DENIR" referenced in TMT (exam-likely fact/trap)

Key Surcharges & Booking Rules (2026)
  • ⚠️ Christmas transport supplement: +50% — applies 6pm on 24 Dec to 6pm on 25 Dec, and 6pm on 31 Dec to 6pm on 1 Jan.
  • ⚠️ Mini-bus assistance mandatory: +€260 — any 6+ pax transfer starting at an airport, train station, or port.
  • 💡 Basque-region night supplement: +10% — transport services 10pm–6am (Bilbao/San Sebastián area transfers specifically call this out, more granular than the general guide-wide night-supplement note elsewhere).
  • 💡 Basque-region weekend/bank holiday supplement: +10% on top of the night supplement where applicable.
  • 💡 Montserrat parking fee — starting 31 Jul 2026, a $35 minivan parking fee (3–6 passengers) applies at the monastery, on top of the tour price.
  • ⚠️ 100% cancellation fee once purchased — Park Güell + Gaudí Experiència combo ticket, and the FC Barcelona Stadium tour. Set this expectation with clients before booking either.
  • 💡 Luggage allowance on all transfers: 1 checked bag + 1 carry-on per person, consistent with the general Arrivals & Transfers guidance below.

Key Surcharges & Booking Rules (2026)
  • ⚠️ Night supplement: +20% (standard 2–14 pax vehicles, 10pm–6am) — this is double Liberty Spain's +10% night supplement. Worth factoring into a DMC choice for a client with a lot of evening/early-morning transfers.
  • 💡 Weekend & Bank Holiday supplement: +10% — consistent with Liberty's rate, but applied more broadly across Spaintop's private-tour line items (many tours have distinct Weekday/Weekend columns; Liberty mostly doesn't).
  • 💡 Airport assistance is priced separately and per-person (see the transfers table above) — don't quote it as a flat €200 the way Liberty's M&G works.
  • 💡 Public holidays & blackout dates follow the same national Spain calendar already documented in the Liberty Spain section above (Holy Week, Feria de Abril, Fallas, San Fermín, etc.) — Spaintop's own tariff confirms the same dates, so no separate calendar is needed here.

Transfer Type Details
Arrival/Departure Flights Arrival points: Madrid, Barcelona, Málaga, Palma de Mallorca; ⚠️ always include a Meet & Greet (M&G) for first arrival — M&G assistant meets at airport or hotel
Domestic Flights Iberia = full-service; Vueling = budget; suggest business-class upgrade; Liberty Spain & Spaintop can book; KT Air books full-service airlines only

Shorter Trains One service level; seats not always assigned; free Wi-Fi; clients stow own luggage; non-refundable tickets
Longer Trains Standard + first-class (assigned seats); first-class sometimes incl. snacks/drinks + Wi-Fi; clients stow own luggage; non-refundable tickets
